item.title: Pentagon quietly prepares for $400 billion cut to Trump's military budget
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Pentagon is quietly preparing for a $400 billion cut to President Donald Trump’s military budget, as officials realize the president’s record-breaking request is effectively dead. The administration has pushed Congress for a supersized $1.5 trillion investment in the military — the largest in history. The money would overhaul weapons stockpiles and realize Trump’s dreams for everything from a sprawling missile shield to a fleet of nuclear-powered battleships . But the Pentagon and congressional spending committees are drafting a smaller $1.1 trillion defense budget, according to a defense industry official, two former officials and one other person familiar with the matter. The planning — which runs contrary to what administration officials are saying publicly — is a clear indication of the political headwinds facing Republicans after the midterm elections. “The Pentagon can’t admit this,” said one of the people who, like the others, was granted anonymity to speak about internal discussions. The administration has hinged its unprecedented defense budget on a party-line process called reconciliation. This would allow Republican lawmakers to add $350 billion to a $1.15 trillion defense base budget, despite objections from Democrats. Now, Pentagon planners are evaluating what defense programs they will be forced to prioritize in the face of reduced funding, the people said. “None of them expect anywhere close to 1.5 trillion,” one of the former officials said. “They are absolutely developing plans [for less] and that is much more the expectation than anything close to 1.5 trillion.” The White House referred questions to the Pentagon, which did not respond to a request for comment. The cuts could scramble the Defense Department’s efforts to procure new weapons platforms, enter into new agreements with the defense industry or even continue existing programs. It could also affect how quickly the U.S. can rebuild weapons stockpiles severely depleted by the Iran war. The Pentagon’s latest estimates show at least $47 billion in costs associated with the conflict, with the lion’s share of that bill, $29 billion, stemming from critical munitions replacements. Trump administration officials have not offered any alternatives — at least not publicly. Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought insisted this month that “we’re not planning on failure.” The administration has not developed alternatives to fund critical Pentagon programs if Congress doesn’t back the White House’s plan, he said. But GOP infighting in both chambers has already imperiled the odds of passing even one piece of the $1.5 trillion total. Top Senate Republicans have warned they don’t have enough votes to pass a party-line spending package. And House Republicans have threatened to withhold their votes over the administration’s handling of foreign policy and a reluctance to devote more money to the military. "Republicans are increasingly angry at the administration on the defense front,” said the former official. It’s “unlikely that anything drastic, a $1.5 trillion budget, would happen.” Lawmakers will return to Washington next month with fewer than five legislative weeks to accomplish a wide range of objectives before the year’s end. If Democrats win control over one or both chambers next week, the GOP will have less than two months to push their priorities through. item.title: Obama-era investigation found evidence against Ilhan Omar's marriage, report says
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn. (Joshua Lott/Getty Images) Federal investigators found evidence during the Obama administration suggesting that Rep. Ilhan Omar's 2009 marriage to a man suspected of being her brother was intended to help him obtain a green card, but the case stalled chiefly because prosecutors concluded the suspected offense fell outside a five-year statute of limitations, according to a new report. The FBI and Department of Homeland Security investigated the marriage in the summer of 2016, current and former officials told The New York Times in a report published Thursday. The officials' account challenges Omar's characterization of the earlier inquiry as having debunked allegations that she married her brother to help him obtain a green card. The newspaper said it remains unclear what evidence investigators had establishing that Omar and her former husband, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, are siblings. Marrying a person to help them obtain a green card is illegal under federal law, while marrying a sibling is illegal under state law. However, the newspaper noted that it remains unclear whether federal prosecutors could pursue charges against Omar despite the statute of limitations for marriage-based immigration fraud. Omar has repeatedly denied the allegations about her and her ex-husband. "Rep. Omar has repeatedly and unequivocally denied this baseless, disgusting conspiracy theory," spokeswoman Jackie Rogers said in a statement. "This is a desperate political smear designed to distract from Trump's failed presidency and two years of Republican failure in Congress." Six current and former officials familiar with the 2016 investigation told the Times that agents found evidence suggesting Omar and Elmi were siblings. The officials said investigators had limited tools to develop the case because prosecutors did not pursue it. Omar was already a U.S. citizen when she married Elmi, a British citizen, in 2009. They divorced in 2017. Two former officials said Elmi obtained a conditional two-year green card through the marriage. When immigration authorities requested additional evidence before granting him permanent status without conditions, he left the United States and abandoned his petition, they said. The earlier inquiry involved an FBI agent specializing in public corruption and civil rights cases and two Homeland Security Investigations agents, according to the report. The allegations surfaced publicly in 2016 as Omar campaigned for a seat in the Minnesota House of Representatives. After a local television station reported that the U.S. attorney's office had opened an investigation, her campaign sought a letter from Andrew Luger, then the U.S. attorney for Minnesota. In the Aug. 22, 2016, letter, Luger wrote that "my office is not investigating, nor have we requested an investigation into Ms. Omar." Omar portrayed the letter as an exoneration that put to rest "flat-out falsehoods." Luger, however, told the Times last week that the letter "was never meant to say anything about the substance of the claims." He said it was intended only to rebut an erroneous report that he had asked ICE to investigate Omar. Luger said federal agents could have been pursuing the matter without his knowledge and denied shielding Omar from scrutiny. The Trump administration has reopened scrutiny of the marriage as part of a broader investigation into the Omar family's immigration history. Federal agents searched the congresswoman's Washington home Oct. 12, weeks before she seeks a fifth term in the House. Investigators are also examining whether Omar's late father submitted false or incomplete information during the immigration process and whether Omar was too old to qualify for citizenship through him in 2000, the Times reported. Democrats have condemned the inquiry as political persecution and said the search violated Justice Department policy intended to prevent investigative actions from influencing elections. President Donald Trump repeated the allegation that Omar married her brother last week. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has said the broader investigation could lead to Omar's deportation if authorities establish that she should not have been admitted to the country. © 2026 Newsmax. item.title: Trump cancels weekend rallies and opts for phone calls as Election Day nears
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
ROCK HILL, S.C. (AP) — President Donald Trump on Thursday canceled weekend rallies in Iowa and Kansas, opting instead to support Republican candidates with telerallies that his party said could reach more voters in nearly two dozen states in the final days of a midterm election that could cost the GOP control of Congress. The president traveled to South Carolina Thursday for the second time in a month, a sign of Republican anxiety about Darline Graham's ability to fend off a robust challenge from Democrat Annie Andrews for a critical U.S. Senate seat. Voters in South Carolina have not sent a Democrat to the Senate in nearly three decades. But Andrews, a pediatrician who previously ran unsuccessfully for Congress , is urging voters seeking change to “try something new for once.” That message could resonate in an election year defined by voter frustration with the economy, gas prices and the war in Iran, putting Trump's Republican Party on defense in territory where they have rarely had to compete in recent years. Beyond South Carolina, Republicans are entering the final days of this year's midterm elections navigating tight contests in Texas, Kansas, Ohio, Iowa and Alaska. Both parties are also closely following developments in the Mississippi Senate race. The president projected confidence as he returned to the White House, saying, “We're going to have a strong Tuesday night.” Trump was scheduled to hold a rally in Kansas on Saturday and in Iowa on Sunday. But the Republican National Committee announced Thursday evening that he would instead spend a “72-hour sprint” doing rallies by phone rather than in person, a move the RNC said would maximize Trump's ability to speak to voters nationwide. The RNC said telerallies are planned for nearly 20 states, and more may be announced. It was an abrupt shift in Trump’s pledge to push through the final days of the campaign doing rally after rally to galvanize his supporters. As of Thursday, he had done 25 rallies during the month of October, falling short of a goal he had once placed north of 30. Trump says he doesn't need to go to Kansas There were signs the travel and long speeches have caught up with him. On Monday, in Corinth, Mississippi, Trump — whose voice has grown raspy — told the crowd, “God didn’t make your vocal cords to do a rally every day.” But he bristled Thursday when a reporter asked whether he had canceled plans to travel to Kansas because of his health. “You’ve been following me for two weeks. I feel perfect,” Trump snapped. The president said he’s not traveling to Kansas, where GOP Sen. Roger Marshall faces Democrat Adam Hamilton, "because he’s doing very well,” an apparent reference to Marshall. “I don’t feel I have to go to Kansas,” Trump said. A campaign strategist with Republican Senate leadership said there was widespread curiosity about why the schedule was changing to telerallies. The strategist spoke on condition of anonymity to share the content of private conversations. Trump, who revels in big crowds, has this month held rallies in smaller venues than many he once filled. The decision to switch to telerallies means he will be expected to speak for about 10 minutes instead of more than 90, as he does at in-person events. Trump plans to travel to Daytona Beach, Florida, for a rally Friday. It’s not clear whether he will hold additional in-person events after that. The White House has not published his schedule for Monday, the final day of the campaign. Democrats took notice. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate candidate in Michigan who's in a tight race against Republican Mike Rogers, said Thursday night that the president's goal of trying to gin up GOP voters has backfired and he has “given up." “He’s an old man, he’s a loser,” El-Sayed continued. “He now understands that he has fully lost the midterms for his party." Graham has struggled to connect with voters In South Carolina, Graham has struggled to quickly build connections with voters. The sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham , she was appointed in July by Republican Gov. Henry McMaster to fill the remaining months of her brother’s term after his sudden death. In August, she became the party’s nominee to succeed him for a full six-year term. “He was a great politician,” Trump said of Lindsey Graham, before promoting Darline Graham as his elected successor. “She’s got the gene.” Darline Graham commended the president for having “delivered what Washington promised for decades.” She warned that Andrews “would just throw it all away." Andrews appeared in nearby Fort Mill on Wednesday, where she said that if voters elect her and become unhappy with her performance on Capitol Hill, “you can fire me in six years.” South Carolina Rep. Ralph Norman, who lost to Graham in the GOP Senate primary runoff , has criticized Graham as unqualified. Norman, who has refused to campaign with Graham, said the race is closer than it would have been had he been nominated. Lonnie Dean Johnson of Sumter, South Carolina, supported Norman in the primary and was voting Graham out of party loyalty, albeit unenthusiastically. “She’s on a Republican ticket. I, by and large, support the Republican platform," he said. "So, I support her and wish her well.” Democrats are bullish about Senate races across the US Democrats, meanwhile, are optimistic about their chances of booting GOP incumbent senators, including in Ohio, with an American public frustrated by continued high costs. “Families see more money going out the door and not enough money coming in,” said Sherrod Brown, the Democratic Senate nominee who's competing against Ohio Republican Sen. Jon Husted. At a rally in Toledo Thursday, Brown said Husted is “looking out for data centers and Wall Street." Farther north, Alaska's Republican governor has ordered an investigation after The New York Times reported Wednesday that Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola's campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting another candidate with the same name as Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan. The Justice Department escalated the investigation Thursday, issuing a raft of new grand jury subpoenas , a person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press. The Justice Department also issued subpoenas to California officials in the latest effort to scrutinize local election administration. A federal judge in California earlier Thursday appointed a special master to evaluate claims by the Trump administration that the state has some 20,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls . Trump called the development in Alaska a “conspiracy” and called for Peltola to be removed from the ballot. He has cast doubt on whether Peltola would be seated in the Senate even if she won the election. Peltola’s campaign didn’t immediately respond to a message Thursday seeking comment on the governor's order. But during a campaign stop in Soldotna, Peltola, a former congresswoman, suggested the Times’ report was a “distraction” from issues such as Sen. Sullivan’s support of the war in Iran . The revelation in Alaska was a reminder of the volatility of the midterm campaigns' final days as both parties make decisions about how to spend time and money with control of Congress on the line. __ Sloan reported from Washington. Associated Press writers Thomas Beaumont in Des Moines, Iowa, Jesse Bedayn in Austin, Texas, Hannah Fingerhut in Clive, Iowa, John Hanna in Topeka, Kansas, Mike Householder in Kalamazoo, Michigan, and Meg Kinnard, Collin Binkley and Alanna Durkin Richer in Washington contributed to this report. This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/trump-lends-support-darline-graham-133116810.html

item.title: Speaker Johnson signals he will keep leading Republicans even if they lose the House
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Speaker Mike Johnson’s (R-La.) recent hints that he intends to remain GOP leader even if Republicans lose the House have rattled the party’s leadership outlook and raised fresh new questions about the GOP’s future heading into the next Congress. Most House Speakers in recent decades have stepped out of Congress after losing the gavel. And Reps. Steve Scalise (R-La.), the majority leader, and Jim Jordan (R-Ohio), a conservative icon, are both expected to launch bids to lead House Republicans if Democrats flip the chamber, according to GOP lawmakers, aides and strategists. But Johnson recently muddled the leadership landscape by signaling his intention to keep his spot atop the party even if Republicans are knocked out of power. Then on Monday, President Trump offered a glowing endorsement of Johnson’s leadership chops, sparking further speculation that Johnson might, in fact, buck historic trends and try to remain leader even from the minority. “Mike Johnson is a true friend, fighter, and WINNER,” Trump posted on social media, “and he has my Complete and Total endorsement for Re-Election.” “Thank you, President @realDonaldTrump!” Johnson responded. “The best is yet to come as we save America!” Much about the leadership race is expected to come into sharper focus after next Tuesday’s midterm elections. A Johnson spokesperson said the Speaker is “solely focused on protecting the majority,” noting that he “will campaign in 21 districts across 13 states between now and Election Day.” But many Republicans are skeptical, predicting Johnson will follow the example of past GOP Speakers — including Newt Gingrich (Ga.), Dennis Hastert (Ill.), Paul Ryan (Wis.) and Kevin McCarthy (Calif.) — who all left Capitol Hill in short order after losing the gavel. “I highly doubt that the Speaker will go for minority leader at this point,” a GOP aide said Wednesday. “I just don't see him having a desire. I don't think he's having a fun time as Speaker. I don't think he'd want to be minority leader.” Former Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) defied modern tradition in 2011, when she clung to the minority leader seat after the party was clobbered in the 2010 midterms. Pelosi would win the gavel back eight years later, but she’s been the exception. GOP strategist Amy Frederiksen said, “When you lose, and you're no longer Speaker …it's hard to go back to minority leader.” “There’s certainly a lot less trappings and a lot less power, and also the caucus just tends to kind of want to clean some house. Like members just see it as an opportunity to just switch things up, and so it's not that it hasn't happened, of course. Speaker Pelosi went to be the minority leader, so it isn't unprecedented,” Frederiksen said. “It wouldn't be historic in any kind of way, and it's very possible. But it is — I don't think it's as simple as him just deciding. I think that the caucus is going to really want to weigh in on things.” She added that Johnson was a “compromise candidate anyway” for Speaker. “We went through a couple, two, three, four different potential Speakers, including Steve Scalise and Jim Jordan, when he was finally chosen as Speaker, so I, you know, I just think that there is that,” she said. “It was sort of a bargain struck anyway for him to be Speaker.” Some Republicans predicted next year’s leadership roster will hinge on how the midterms play out. Although Trump is not on the ballot, the elections are shaping up to be a referendum on the president, whose historic unpopularity has created huge challenges for GOP candidates and made Democrats the favorite to control the House next year. Still, some Republicans believe that if Democrats win by a wide margin, Johnson will bear much of the blame, lose support within the conference and struggle to secure the votes needed to become minority leader, even if Trump wanted him there. “I would imagine there to be more of a push for someone else, just given that over, you know, a billion dollars has been spent on the midterms alone,” a second GOP staffer, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, told The Hill earlier this month. Although both Scalise and Jordan have downplayed their interest in the top spot, many Republicans say they’re both angling for the position, setting the stage for a potentially messy internal fight when House lawmakers return to Washington the week after the midterms. (Minnesota Rep. Tom Emmer, the Republican whip, says he wants to remain in that seat). There’s plenty of disagreement about who would have the advantage in such a race. Some say that if it’s a two-way race between Scalise and Jordan, Scalise would likely be better positioned than Jordan to step into the top spot given his current leadership position. “I think for Scalise … it'd be an easy transition for him to step into that. But for Jordan, he's really — how do I phrase this? He's been a loyal soldier. He's rallied people well, and he's an effective politician. So I think both would do well in the role, but I think Scalise would have an easier transition just out of pure — his House leadership currently,” a third GOP staffer said. The first Republican staffer, though, predicted Jordan has the edge. “He's done a lot of work over the past couple years where he's kind of built his own coalition, [and] he does have, like, a cult following around the country when he goes on the campaign trail. So I do think it's his to lose at this point,” the first aide said. “When you're in the minority, you need somebody who can be a fighter and willing to go out there and go on TV and bomb some bombs. And I think he's the guy for it.” The offices of Scalise and Jordan did not respond to requests for comment on Wednesday. Johnson has faced a rocky tenure as Speaker, often marked by internal GOP fighting, a razor-thin margin and repeated challenges in keeping his conference united on government spending, the Iran war and other issues. Even so, Johnson told CBS News’s Robert Costa this month that in the “unlikely scenario” Republicans lose the House, “I would expect my colleagues would ask me to continue leading this conference, even if we have divided government.” “I’m going to continue to serve my highest best use to God and country, and I believe right now, as we’re sitting here, that’s the Speaker of the House,” Johnson said. “And if we lost the majority, I don’t think that that position that I have would change. I think I would stay right there.” Some Republicans note that if Johnson were to jump into the minority leader race, he would have a strong case for the position. The third GOP staffer noted Johnson’s “had to deal with a lot of curveballs” and that he’s handled them well. “I think that the party recognizes that and will react accordingly,” the staffer said. “That doesn't mean there's not people gunning for the same spot, but I think Johnson has been a good leader, a team player amidst what is, you know — we could say honestly — has been some chaos at times.” Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. item.title: Pentagon accuses fired 3-star general of leaking classified information
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
(Sgt. Timothy Jackson/U.S. Army/Associated Press) Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia, a Pentagon senior military startegist, admitted disclosing classified information about Iran and Ukraine to journalists, according to an internal investigation report obtained by Axios. The report details contacts between Sylvia and two reporters from different news organizations over roughly a year, including encrypted communications and a meeting at a restaurant in Arlington, Virginia, where he allegedly relayed information from a classified document. War Secretary Pete Hegseth fired Sylvia following an investigation into unauthorized disclosures. A U.S. official told Axios that Sylvia acknowledged the misconduct in a recorded interview after failing four polygraph examinations. Reuters and CBS News cited Pentagon officials who said Sylvia failed three examinations. The allegations also have been disputed by some of Sylvia's colleagues. One told The Washington Post that the general repeatedly denied leaking classified information, although he acknowledged having contact with journalists. Sylvia headed the Joint Staff's Directorate for Strategy, Plans and Policy, known as J5, which helps develop military strategy and advise the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. According to Axios, the investigation traced Sylvia's contacts with reporters to at least June 2025. Some communications reportedly occurred through the encrypted messaging application Signal, while another encounter took place at a Silver Diner in Arlington after a journalist lost access to the Pentagon under tightened press restrictions. During that meeting, Sylvia allegedly used notes taken from a classified report to brief a journalist on U.S. assistance to Ukraine. The investigator's report said the journalist was working on a book and had met with Sylvia twice. The general had not obtained authorization from the Pentagon's public affairs office or arranged for the material to be reviewed before sharing it, according to the report. Investigators also examined deleted Signal communications involving another reporter and discussions concerning Iran. Sylvia reportedly said he had deleted a message without responding and believed he had inadvertently erased the entire conversation. U.S. officials, however, suspected the deletion was deliberate, Axios reported. The investigation also found that Sylvia acknowledged being among 20 officials cited in a news report critical of Pentagon leadership. The report described Sylvia as cooperative during questioning and said he surrendered his personal phone for forensic examination. Questions about Sylvia's removal also prompted an unusual reversal by the Joint Staff, which initially issued a statement thanking him for his 32 years of military service before withdrawing it. A U.S. official told Axios that acting Army Secretary Adam Telle's office had pushed for the favorable statement to limit potential fallout from allegations involving classified information. The Joint Staff subsequently withdrew its remarks after learning more about the circumstances of Sylvia's dismissal. Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said Thursday that an investigation by the Air Force Office of Special Investigations had prompted personnel action to safeguard sensitive information. He also said the matter, along with others, had been referred to the Justice Department for possible legal action. Sylvia, a decorated combat veteran who previously commanded the Army's 101st Airborne Division, did not respond to requests for comment from Axios and other news organizations. His removal comes as President Donald Trump considers renewed military strikes against Iran. A Pentagon official told The Associated Press that Sylvia was not a central planner of the Iran conflict, saying those responsibilities belonged to U.S. Central Command. The allegations arise during a broader Pentagon effort to identify unauthorized disclosures. In July, Hegseth announced a joint initiative with the Justice Department targeting leaks, while stricter media-access rules introduced last year prompted numerous news organizations to surrender their Pentagon credentials. © 2026 Newsmax. All rights reserved.This article originally appeared on Newsmax at https://www.newsmax.com/newsfront/brett-sylvia-pentagon-army/2026/10/29/id/1274518

item.title: Crypto exchange Binance freezes assets after $6.3 billion security breach
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Ankur Banerjee, Tom Westbrook and Summer Zhen SINGAPORE/HONG KONG Oct 30 (Reuters) - Hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, in what analysts say is the biggest crypto hack ever, an attack that could prompt investors to rethink the risks of owning digital assets. The hackers behind the raid were from North Korea, according to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and ‌Chainalysis. The attackers targeted Binance wallets on 10 blockchains and shifted most of the funds in about 20 minutes, TRM Labs said in a statement. Binance said it worked with partners to freeze the affected ‌assets with about $3 billion located so far. It did not mention the status of the remaining $3.3 billion, and its co-founder Yi He said the exchange would cover "all hacking losses". Binance said its deposits were unaffected and it expects to resume withdrawal services in the next 48 hours. TRM said ​several features of the attack matched earlier heists linked to North Korea, including a 2025 hack of crypto exchange Bybit that the US Federal Bureau of Investigation had attributed to Pyongyang. "We make this judgment with high confidence," it said in a statement. North Korea’s mission in Geneva and its embassy in China did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment. The incident could be the world's biggest crypto heist, according to analytics firm Chainalysis and other industry experts. "It's the biggest hack in history," said Aravind Srinivasan, head of large crypto market maker GSR's systematic OTC business. Markets reacted immediately in Asian trading on Friday. Bitcoin dropped more than 3% to a six-week low of $76,368 and ether fell more than 3% to a two-month low of $2,178. BNB, ‌a token originally launched as Binance Coin that can be used to pay Binance ⁠fees, was down 5% over the past 24 hours at $709.70, according to market aggregator CoinGecko. Shares in crypto exchange Coinbase Global slid 4.8% while those of bitcoin buyer Strategy fell nearly 6% in extended US trading. HACKED LAPTOP An initial investigation suggested the breach may have started with a hacked laptop belonging to one of its engineers, which let an attacker gain ⁠access to one of its systems and make unauthorized withdrawals, Binance said. "The incident stems from multiple factors. Our security team is tracing the full attack path through the compromised computer which may be the entry point of the incident," Binance said. Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for crypto, which had already been under pressure due to higher US interest rates and softer demand from exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said. "It may further dampen risk appetite and prompt investors ​to ​reassess the safety of assets held on centralized exchanges, as well as counterparty, solvency and liquidity risks," said Tim Sun, senior ​researcher at HashKey Group, based in Hong Kong. Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and ‌trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about $162.8 billion in assets under custody as of the exchange's 2025 annual report. "User funds remain safe," Binance said in a statement. BINANCE HAS SECURE ASSET FUND Binance runs a secure asset fund for users, which is a reserve held entirely in bitcoin that is intended to protect user assets in cases of security breaches, according to its website. "It's becoming very hard to counter hacks as AI can find vulnerabilities faster than you can fix them," said Bernardo Brites, CEO of Trace Finance, a payments and stablecoin infrastructure company. "My view is that users will move away from smaller and medium-sized exchanges, (it is) becoming too risky to park your money somewhere that couldn't cover a hack of meaningful size." Stablecoin issuer Tether said it had frozen nearly $1.57 billion in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800 million. World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to US President ‌Donald Trump and his family, said on Thursday it had worked with cryptocurrency custodian BitGo to freeze funds stolen in what ​it described as a Binance hack. Binance's Yi said $27 million in stablecoins and about $2 million worth of World Liberty tokens had been frozen. Crypto ​firm Ripple also froze roughly $200 million in funds, Yi said. Jack McDonald, senior vice president of stablecoins ​at Ripple, said the company was closely monitoring reports of a potential exploit involving Binance and was freezing affected funds and coordinating with relevant parties. INCIDENT ADDS TO STRING OF CRYPTO THEFTS Miguel ‌Morel, CEO of blockchain intelligence firm Arkham, said data indicated that billions of dollars ​appeared to have been hacked from Binance by an unknown ​actor. The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year, attackers stole $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs. In September, cryptocurrency exchange Bitget said roughly $350 million in crypto had been stolen from its platform, underscoring the industry's vulnerability to hackers. Authorities have warned that organised crime groups are increasingly using cryptocurrencies to move funds across borders outside the traditional financial system. Binance.US, a ​separate cryptocurrency exchange, said it was not affected by the security incident. Coinbase said it ‌was unaffected and was monitoring the situation. In an unrelated incident earlier on Thursday, prediction market operator Polymarket temporarily halted trading after a security incident involving a third-party provider. It later resumed trading ​and said it would fully reimburse affected traders. (Reporting by Tom Westbrook, Ankur Banerjee and Rae Wee in Singapore, Summer Zhen in Hong Kong, Vallari Srivastava and Anusha Shah in Bengaluru and Mrinmay ​Dey in Mexico City; Writing by Scott Murdoch; Editing by Michelle Price, Sherry Jacob-Phillips, Jamie Freed and Stephen Coates) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/crypto/articles/tether-circle-freeze-2-38-222607515.html

item.title: El-Sayed and Stevens to make rare joint appearance as Dems seek unity in Michigan
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
DETROIT (AP) — Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed will campaign Sunday in Detroit alongside former primary rival Rep. Haley Stevens, marking their first public appearance together in months after a week in which lingering divisions spilled into public view. The two will be joined by South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn, one of the country's most prominent Black politicians, at a get-out-the-vote event at a Detroit church, according to two people familiar with the plans who were not authorized to discuss them publicly. The event was first reported by The Associated Press. The joint appearance — their first since a Democratic unity breakfast days after the Aug. 4 primary — follows weeks of Democrats struggling to unite behind El-Sayed following his razor-thin victory over Stevens. She received significant support from the Jewish and Black communities, leading to concerns about turnout in the general election. Tensions again spilled into public view Wednesday when Stevens' fiancé, Jason Turkish, told The Detroit News that he would vote for Republican Mike Rogers . Hours later, Stevens appeared on CNN to reaffirm that she would be voting for El-Sayed, but urged his campaign to “shut out the hate and call it out.” She said El-Sayed needs to reach out to people who were part of her coalition and “make them feel comfortable about coming to the polls.” Asked Thursday evening about the upcoming event with Stevens, El-Sayed said “we’re always trying to unify the party” and it hadn’t happened sooner because of their busy schedules. El-Sayed then criticized the reporter for the question, saying “nobody cares” about internal party dynamics when the cost of living is so high. While significant, the joint appearance comes just days before the election El-Sayed and Stevens last appeared together on Aug. 6, two days after the primary. Stevens pledged to support El-Sayed, telling CBS News she would do “whatever he wants me to do” on the campaign trail. But divisions from the contentious primary have persisted. Nearly $60 million was spent on advertising attacking El-Sayed, including $30 million from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC. Stevens is a staunch supporter of Israel who represents a district with a large Jewish community in Detroit’s suburbs. The church visit on Sunday is intended to further that elusive unity, although its impact is uncertain, given that it comes just two days before the election. Michigan early voting started Oct. 24. “We’ve got a Black and Jewish coalition that came out and voted for me in droves. And I want them to come out and vote for Democrats," Stevens said to CNN on Wednesday. El-Sayed's criticism of Israel, past remarks and his association with controversial streamer Hasan Piker have long drawn concern from some in Michigan's large Jewish community. Turkish and others have said El-Sayed hasn't done enough to address concerns ahead of the general election. The latest controversy centered on an ad by Rebellion PAC, an independent left-wing group, that linked U.S. support for Israel to high grocery prices. “That has nothing to do with our campaign,” El-Sayed said of the ad. “It’s certainly not what I want to be talking about right now.” Stevens and other Democrats urged him to go further to denounce the content of the advertisement rather than merely distancing himself from it. Trump’s rhetoric and actions create challenges for Republicans. Republicans face political challenges of their own, particularly voter dissatisfaction with Trump, the Iran war and high costs. Rogers has remained closely aligned with the president on most issues, appearing alongside him at a Michigan rally Sunday where he credited Trump with bringing manufacturing jobs back to the state. The rally took place in Port Huron, just across the river from Canada, a country with deep economic ties to Michigan that Trump has targeted with tariffs. El-Sayed has held campaign events in heavily Republican areas, including Michigan’s Upper Peninsula. His team also released an ad featuring clips of prominent conservative figures praising him, including former Fox News host Tucker Carlson, who has faced accusations of antisemitism that he denies. But the ad created another source of friction with some Jewish voters. Rabbi Aaron Starr of Congregation Shaarey Zedek in Southfield criticized both the Rebellion PAC ad and El-Sayed’s campaign ad during a call with reporters. “We are one week away from the election, and it feels like the temperature has turned way up,” Starr said. “Instead of things getting better over the last seven weeks, they’ve actually gotten worse.” Rogers, meanwhile, appeared Wednesday with Republican Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas at an event hosted by the Republican Jewish Coalition in Birmingham, Michigan. Cruz called antisemitism “a poison that is ripping the country apart” and accused Democrats of being taken over by “self-proclaimed communists and Islamists.” Trump has repeatedly attacked El-Sayed’s Muslim faith, calling him a “jihadist” and saying Sunday that he was “on the side of terrorists.” Both campaigns make a final push for Black voters Both candidates are trying to win over Black voters, particularly in Detroit's Wayne County, where Stevens defeated El-Sayed in the Democratic primary. El-Sayed's event with Stevens and Clyburn is part of an effort to shore up support among Black voters. Much of El-Sayed's final campaign stretch has included appearances in Detroit. Rogers has also sought to make inroads with Black voters. He visited a reading remediation program at a Detroit high school and discussed housing costs with residents in Pontiac, north of the city. Earlier this month, his wife handed out $10 gift cards at a gas station. The gesture drew criticism from Ruby Farmer, a 68-year-old Detroit retiree. “You’re giving out gas cards in the inner city; you never would come for any other reason,” Farmer said. While Farmer has a bit of difficulty pronouncing El-Sayed's name, she cast her ballot for him three weeks ago anyways. El-Sayed has come out in opposition to policies by Trump — policies Farmer says directly impact her family. “I have a special-needs son,” said Farmer. “He depends on Medicaid. Medicaid has been cut, and for home care workers in Michigan, all the benefits are on hold.” ___ Cappelletti reported from Washington. Mike Householder contributed from Kalamazoo, Michigan. item.title: Netanyahu has no majority in Israel's election, but time may be on his side
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
CNN Israel faces weeks, possibly months, of political limbo after final results show there’s no clear winner in its elections . Neither of the two main blocs – one led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud party, the other led by the centrist Yashar party of his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot – have reached the required 61-seat majority to form a government in Israel’s 120-seat parliament. So how could a new government be formed? Certainly, it does not look easy, with deep-rooted political and ideological divisions making any seemingly straightforward coalition almost impossible. Still, it can be done, even if the result is a tenuous alliance that survives little more than a year or so in office. If party leaders are unable to figure it out in the 12 weeks they will have available, then Israelis will be back at the polls. Here’s some potential scenarios that could avoid that. Scenario 1: An opposition government On paper, the opposition’s surest path to unseat Netanyahu is built on Jewish-Arab cooperation. And that is its biggest obstacle. Two of the opposition bloc’s right-wing party leaders, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett and former Defense Minister Avigdor Liberman, oppose any government that depends on the two Arab parties in parliament – the Joint List and Raam – whether it’s from inside the coalition, or as outside supporters of a minority government. The two leaders have hardened their positions since the Hamas-led attack of October 7, 2023. Only one government in Israel’s history has enjoyed the full participation of an Arab party. Raam was part of an eight-party coalition that succeeded in ousting Netanyahu in 2021, but it collapsed just after a year in office. Even without forming a government, the opposition parties could still work together and leverage their parliamentary majority to replace the Knesset speaker, along with other key positions, and thereby constrain Netanyahu’s caretaker government as it continued in power. But the prospects of assembling a coalition to replace him as Israel’s leader remain highly complicated and politically charged. Scenario 2: A national unity government Another option would see the implosion of the two blocs in favor of a unity government. Netanyahu’s Likud party would certainly be involved, along with some of his existing coalition partners, as well as – crucially – at least one party from the opposition bloc. Netanyahu, in this case, is believed to be willing to part ways with his far-right National Security Minister Ben-Gvir – but not from far-right Finance Minister Bezazel Smotrich and the ultra-Orthodox parties. Eisenkot , however, has ruled out sitting with Netanyahu, and it would be seen by many Israelis desperate to see the back of ‘Bibi’ as an act of betrayal if he were to change his mind. Scenario 3: A Netanyahu bloc government with defectors Another scenario could see Netanyahu encouraging defections from opposition parties or individual lawmakers. But all four opposition bloc party leaders – Eisenkot, Bennett, Liberman and Yair Golan – have declared they will not sit with him. And with Netanyahu’s bloc a full eight seats short, persuading eight individual defectors sets a high bar. Scenario 4: Another election While all these possibilities are being discussed in the background, Israeli President Isaac Herzog will hold a very public round of consultations with the leaders of the parties that have made it into parliament. Once he has solicited their opinions, he will task one of those leaders with the job of trying to form a government. Arab parties are expected to voice their support for Eisenkot, so the Yashar leader could be asked to go first. Whoever gets the nod will have 28 days to complete the job, with a possible 14-day extension if needed. If it all comes to nothing, the president will ask a second leader to have a go. They get 28 days only to sort it out. After that, a majority of Knesset members could ask the president to task a third candidate, who then has 14 days to build a coalition. If none of these produce a breakthrough, there will be another election. The person who appears best-placed to navigate this timetable is Netanyahu. As caretaker prime minister, he can afford to wait: If main rival Eisenkot gets the first shot – and fails – the mandate is likely to pass to him. And if he fails as well, the political deadlock seems certain to lead Israel to another round of elections – with Netanyahu remaining caretaker for months, until another government is formed. A repeat election – which would happen no earlier than next spring – is a real possibility, as these results look set to return Israel to a state of political paralysis and what would be the seventh general election in eight years. item.title: Biggest changes in nearly 30 years could be coming to baby formula
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) announced on Thursday it is proposing a new rule that will update the nutrient requirements for infant formula. The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), which oversees the FDA, said in a press release that it would be the first major update to infant formula standards in nearly 30 years. Abbott launches new infant formula made with whole milk: What parents need to know The proposed rule would update requirements for vitamin A, vitamin D, iodine and manganese as well as reaffirm existing requirements for chloride, potassium, selenium and sodium, the agencies said. It would also change the units of measure for two nutrients and request public input on possible requirements for ingredients not currently required in infant formula but sometimes added by manufacturers, they noted. The ingredients not currently required include arachidonic acid (ARA), docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), and L-carnitine. Some studies have suggested they contribute greatly to infant growth, brain development and health. Andrew Harnik/AP Photo, FILE - PHOTO: In this Oct. 14, 2015, file photo, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration campus is shown in Silver Spring, Md. The agency said there will be additional phases looking at the remaining required nutrients, potential new nutrient requirements and carbohydrate sources. The FDA said it will welcome public comment during its phases and, in the future, will issue one final rule to cover all the proposed changes. The FDA also released new data on chemical contaminant testing for infant formula and found that most samples tested had "low or non-detectable levels of chemical contaminants." "Parents deserve confidence in every bottle they feed their baby," HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. said in a statement, in part. "We will hold infant formula manufacturers to rigorous scientific standards and put babies' health first." Last year, the HHS and FDA announced they would review the nutrition quality of infant formula in the U.S. CDC says 51 infants hospitalized in botulism outbreak amid ByHeart voluntary formula recall The FDA said the review -- part of its "Operation Stork Speed" initiative -- would look at whether current nutrient requirements need to be updated, including whether additional nutrients need to be considered. Under current law, the HHS secretary reviews the table of required nutrients every four years as appropriate. The FDA currently specifies 30 nutrients that must be included in infant formulas. There are minimum amounts for all 30 nutrients and maximum amounts for 10 nutrients, according to the agency. Among the nutrients currently required are protein and fat, as well as vitamins A, D, E, K, folic acid, iron, magnesium and zinc. Oscar Wong/STOCK PHOTO/Getty Images - PHOTO: Stock photo of an infant receiving formula. Last year, then-FDA commissioner Dr. Marty Makary discussed removing seed oils from infant formulas. Many commercial baby formulas contain seed or vegetable oils due to the essential fatty acids they provide. "Generally, they're believed to be pro-inflammatory," Makary said of seed oils during an interview on "Fox & Friends" in June 2025. "We don't want babies with general body inflammation. Forty percent of our nation's kids have a chronic condition. Many of those are tied to inflammation and insulin resistance." Doctors have previously told ABC News that seed oils are not pro-inflammatory and can help lower glucose levels, improve insulin sensitivity, reduce bad (LDL) cholesterol, reduce triglycerides and increase levels of positive (HDL) cholesterol. ABC News' Katie Kindelan contributed to this report. This article originally appeared on ABC News at https://abcnews.com/Health/fda-proposes-rule-updating-nutrient-requirements-infant-formula/story?id=137680100

item.title: Peltola denies knowing about Alaska spoiler candidate as DOJ issues new subpoenas
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola denied Thursday that she knew anything about an effort to put another candidate on the Alaska ballot with the same name as the Republican incumbent as the Justice Department escalated a criminal investigation with new grand jury subpoenas. “I just want to clear the air," she said at the top of a speech in a downtown bar in Juneau, Alaska’s capital. “I knew nothing about any other candidate on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about. I am not interested in tricking voters." Peltola is running against Sen. Dan Sullivan. A person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press that subpoenas seeking grand jury testimony or documents, along with records preservation demands, were issued after The New York Times reported that Peltola’s campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan Jr. as part of an alleged effort to confuse voters. The race is considered key to control of the U.S. Senate. More subpoenas were expected, according to the person who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the ongoing probe. Neither the recipients of the subpoenas nor the number of them were immediately clear. The Justice Department for months has been looking into allegations that Dan J. Sullivan Jr. entered the race to siphon votes from the incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan. The potential targets of the investigation are unclear, but President Donald Trump earlier this week called for the criminal prosecution of Peltola and her campaign. Attorney General Todd Blanche in a Fox News interview on Wednesday said he wouldn’t discuss any criminal investigations, but accused Democrats of “cheating.” “They are trying to take votes away from the incumbent, not by running an election, not by running on issues but by putting up a person with the same name,” Blanche said. Dan J. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats’ behest and has said he had no contact with Peltola’s campaign. “Zero, none, zilch,” he said in June after announcing his run. The race is among a handful of Senate contests this year expected to determine control of the chamber. Trump had previously directed his Department of Justice to sue to block certification of the Senate race should Democrat Mary Peltola defeat Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. State attorneys asked a court to rule on the Justice Department’s lawsuit by Monday, saying the case could “cast a cloud over Alaska’s election that is contrary to the public interest.” Alaska's Republican governor has also ordered an investigation Separately, Republican Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy has ordered an investigation into Peltola, saying the newspaper's reporting “reveals disturbing new evidence of an organized effort to manipulate Alaska’s elections by recruiting candidates — including one with the same name as an incumbent U.S. Senator — to deliberately confuse voters and misdirect their votes.” “Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections,” Dunleavy added, noting that the reporting “substantially supports” earlier findings by the state’s elections board into the matter. Trump on Thursday cast doubt on whether Peltola would be seated in the Senate even if she won the election. “Well, you’re going to have to see what happens," the president told reporters on his way to a rally in South Carolina. "It’s hard to believe that she could even be allowed to run.” Later, as he rallied for Republican Sen. Darline Graham, Trump said he felt Peltola “actually should be removed from the ballot and prosecuted." Peltola dismisses the claims as a ‘distraction’ Peltola alluded to the controversy in a fundraising post Thursday. “They can’t win on their record so they’re trying to intimidate me into backing down,” she said, adding later: “This is just another distraction as they avoid answering for the skyrocketing cost of living we’re facing because of their tariffs and forever wars. It won’t work.” In Juneau, Alaska, independent Carter Bancroft said he voted Thursday for Peltola. “I’m very certain in the candidates I wanted to vote for and I wanted to vote for Mary Peltola,” he said. But he said the latest claims have bothered him. He worries they give “ammunition” to Trump and others to attack Peltola or other Democratic candidates. “And I think I’m bothered by shenanigans on either side," Bancroft said, especially actions intended “to confuse things or try to trick people.” John Delgado, an independent who leans Republican, said he has “warmed up” to Sen. Sullivan, especially in light of the recent claims. He agrees that Peltola should drop out of the race. The situation in Alaska isn't that unusual. Political parties often support extra candidates on ballots to try to pull votes from their rivals. If state courts allow it, legal experts say, the federal government has no role challenging the results. In Ohio’s Senate race, Republicans have been tied to an effort to boost a socialist on the ballot who would pull votes from the Democratic candidate challenging Sen. Jon Husted. On Thursday, Vice President JD Vance didn’t go as far as Trump did in calling for Peltola to be prosecuted but said he supported a probe into possible election fraud. “I mean, she is a person who, for months now, has pretended that she has had nothing to do with the fact that they have put a fraudulent person, a person explicitly designed to confuse Alaska voters, on the ballot,” Vance told reporters ahead of a campaign trip to Texas. “She is trying to steal a Senate seat from the voters of Alaska, and it’s disgraceful.” State Supreme Court OK'd the other Sullivan on the ballot Earlier this year, a top state elections official ruled Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired schoolteacher in the small fishing community of Petersburg, ineligible for the primary ballot , concluding that his declaration of candidacy was filed “with a purpose to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballot’s fairness or neutrality.” The case went to the Alaska Supreme Court, which ruled he was qualified to run. Alaskan voters will see “Dan S. Sullivan” identified as a “registered Republican” and “incumbent” on their ballots, while “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.” will not have a party affiliation. The New York Times reported that interviews, text messages and documents prepared for a potential lawsuit showed Peltola’s team aimed to coax candidates into the race, with the aim of splitting support for the GOP senator. Asked about the reporting on Wednesday, Trump told journalists, “I think they should be prosecuted.” He earlier had posted on social media that “Peltola should suffer the Legal and Political consequences for what she has done.” ___ Associated Press writer Seung Min Kim contributed to this report. item.title: Vivek Ramaswamy's ad using Amy Acton's estranged mother has ended its TV run
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Many, including term-limited Gov. Mike DeWine, a Republican who has endorsed Vivek Ramaswamy, pictured, had called on him to take down the ad. (Jon Cherry / AP) Republican Vivek Ramaswamy’s ad featuring the estranged mother of Amy Acton, his Democratic opponent for Ohio governor, is leaving the state’s airwaves, the Ramaswamy campaign confirmed Thursday. The ad, which debuted last week to wide bipartisan condemnation, is rotating out after completing its intended run, according to the campaign. The campaign has other ads running in the final days of the race. In the now-completed ad campaign, Donna Arthur — the mother whom Acton says she has not seen since her then-stepfather was charged with raping her as a young child nearly 50 years ago — calls her daughter a liar and urges Ohioans not to vote for her. The ad does not address details of the rape case. But critics panned the Ramaswamy campaign’s decision to use Arthur as a character witness and dredge up painful family history. “I’m learning things even about my childhood right now that I did not know,” Acton told reporters Tuesday during a campaign stop in Youngstown. “I think it is despicable. … I’m sure someday I’ll unpack everything that I’m learning here. But I’m just grateful to Ohioans and everyone, really so much support and love that we’ve received.” The Ramaswamy campaign said last week that the ad would be backed by $4 million in airtime. It began as a minutelong spot but was eventually shortened to a 30-second version. Many, including term-limited Gov. Mike DeWine , a Republican who has endorsed Ramaswamy, had called on him to take down the ad. “Vivek Ramaswamy should never have run his despicable ad in the first place, and it’s totally unsurprising that he took it off the air in the most cowardly way possible, without even the hint of an apology to Dr. Acton, her family, or to the people of Ohio,” Acton campaign spokesperson Addie Bullock said in a statement Thursday. The Columbus Dispatch first reported that the ad was ending its run. “It ran to completion, and we’ve put up four other ads,” Ramaswamy said at a Thursday campaign stop, according to the newspaper.
